title: Emit-windowed handoff & throttling experiments
content:
Purpose:

Short: capture an experimental design for a hybrid handoff that limits decode-side interference with ongoing prefill microbatches by introducing an emit-windowed gating and soft-throttles when kernel pressure or KV residency risk increases.

Why this doc exists (context):
- We see tail latency regressions when heavy prefill microbatching coincides with bursty interactive decode streams (streaming chat).
- Existing proposals focus on global priority lanes or strict prefill preemption; both have tradeoffs: strict preemption improves streaming latency but kills throughput; pure priority lanes are brittle when kernel utilization shifts.
- Goal: find a middle-ground behavior that's robust across load shapes and straightforward to instrument/rollback.

Goals and success metrics:
- Primary outcome: reduce 95/99th percentile streaming token latency by >=20% under mixed workloads while keeping host GPU throughput loss <=8% for steady-state batched prefill workloads.
- Secondary: reduce KV-cache churn (measured as percent of evicted KV entries per minute) and prevent repeated cold-KV penalties for hot sessions.
- Operational: solution must be toggleable per-host and visible in Console (route-level metrics and a simple boolean).

Assumptions:
- Prefill kernels are more compute-dense and can sustain slightly higher GPU usage per token than decode (due to larger matrix ops); decode is latency-sensitive and benefits from low jitter.
- KV residency matters most for long context history sessions (chat threads) and for multi-turn completions where prefill eviction leads to re-prefill penalties.
- We have fine-grained metrics: per-stream token emit time, per-batch kernel occupancy, KV hit/miss rates, per-host GPU SM utilization.

Proposal summary (high-level):
- Emit-windowed handoff: each decode stream maintains a sliding emit window (EW) that bounds how many tokens may be emitted continuously without yielding to pending prefill microbatches.
- Soft-throttle: when per-host kernel pressure or KV eviction risk crosses thresholds, newly arriving decode tokens are delayed by a short, randomized backoff instead of immediate preemption.
- Microbatch alignment: align prefill microbatches to small quanta (configurable: 16, 32 tokens) so handoffs have deterministic points where the host can accept short decode bursts.
- Priority decays: streams accumulate priority credit when idle; credit can be spent to win short emit windows. Credit decay prevents starvation of prefill.

Detailed behaviors and heuristics:
1) Emit Window (EW) definition and lifecycle:
   - EW is measured in tokens and time (two knobs). Default: token EW = 8 tokens, time EW = 50ms, whichever triggers first.
   - When a stream begins emitting, EW is granted immediately if host load < soft_threshold. If load >= soft_threshold, grant is probabilistic (p = 0.3) and may apply a randomized small delay (5-15ms).
   - After EW expires, stream yields: either get queued behind one microbatch boundary or get a short SRR (short round-robin) slot to check again.

2) Soft-throttle and host state machine:
   - Host-level metrics used: kernel_util_pct (rolling 1s), kv_eviction_rate (per-minute), decode_emit_queue_length.
   - Soft_threshold: kernel_util_pct > 78% OR kv_eviction_rate > 2% per minute triggers soft-throttle.
   - In soft-throttle: EW size is reduced (default to 4 tokens), grant probability reduced, and decode arrivals are delayed by random(4..12)ms before admission.
   - Hard-throttle: kernel_util_pct > 92% OR kv_eviction_rate > 6%/min => prefill microbatches preempt decode immediately for one microbatch quantum. Hard-throttle rarely entered; require confirmation over 200ms window.

3) Microbatch alignment and prefetch windows:
   - Prefill microbatches are sliced into quanta of Q tokens (experiment with Q = 8, 16, 32). Hosts will expose microbatch boundaries to the admission controller.
   - When a decode stream yields, it is re-enqueued to the next microbatch boundary. This reduces mid-microbatch context switches and kernel thrash.

4) KV residency protection:
   - Hot-session tag: sessions with KV hit-rate > 85% and > 100 tokens of context are considered hot. For hot sessions, EW grants are biased (higher probability) even under soft-throttle, but EW size is limited to avoid thrashing.
   - When kv_eviction_rate exceeds threshold, we preferentially schedule prefill microbatches that touch the hottest keys (LRU-weighted).

5) Priority credits and fairness:
   - Each stream accumulates credit while waiting or when it had low recent CPU (simple leaky-bucket). Credit allows occasional larger EWs (burst tokens).
   - Prefill workloads can accumulate counter-credits when they are delayed; if prefill delay exceeds T_delay (default 200ms), prefill priority is boosted to avoid head-of-line starvation.

Experiment plan (what to run):
- Controlled bench: 3 host types: small (A100-sim), medium (H100-sim), large (multi-GPU lane) with synthetic load generator.
- Workloads:
  * Mix 1: 70% prefill throughput (avg 128-token prefill), 30% streaming (interactive chat; bursts of 12 tokens at 100ms intervals).
  * Mix 2: 50/50 with heavier long-context hot sessions.
  * Mix 3: streaming-dominant bursts (80% streaming bursts).
- Parameter sweep: EW tokens = [4,8,12], EW time = [30ms, 50ms, 80ms], Q = [8,16,32], soft_threshold kernel_util = [70%,78%,85%].
- Compare strategies: baseline (current preemption logic), strict-preempt (prefill always wins), lane-priority (dedicated fast lane for streams), EW+soft-throttle (this proposal).

Metrics to collect per run:
- Per-route: p50/p95/p99 token latency for streaming routes.
- Prefill throughput: tokens/sec, average batch completion time.
- KV metrics: eviction rate, hit-rate per session, re-prefill count (prefill required because KV entry evicted).
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, kernel switch frequency, average kernel time slice.
- QoS violations: percent of requests missing SLO.

Data and instrumentation requirements:
- New host metrics: kv_eviction_rate (agg per minute), kernel_switch_freq (per-second), EW_grant_log (per-event small payload).
- Trace link: each admission decision should attach a short trace id to correlate eventual latency.
- Console dashboard: route-level EW grants, host soft/hard-throttle state transitions, kv_eviction heatmap.

Rollback and safety plan:
- Feature gate per-host with server-side kill-switch. Default off for critical clusters.
- Canary rollout: 5% hosts for 24h, monitor p99 and KV eviction. Auto rollback rule: p99_streaming increases > 10% absolute OR kv_eviction_rate > 3% in canary.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Complexity: more admission logic could be harder to debug; mitigated by rich logs and simple defaults.
- Starvation: poorly tuned credit system could let prefill backpressure build; experiments must track fairness indicators.
- Oscillation: host-level thresholds may cause thrash between soft/hard states — add hysteresis and confirm windows.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should EW be per-token or per-step (model step sometimes emits multiple tokens)? Need to map to runtime kernel boundaries.
- Optimal Q: smaller Q reduces latency for streams but increases kernel overhead—what's the knee for H100?
- How do we incorporate quantized kernel variants where per-token cost differs and impacts optimal EW?
- Implementation sketch: who owns admission controller? runtime scheduler or orchestrator shim? (Owner: Miguel to propose by 2024-11-12).
- Add synthetic workload for long-tailed chat (10k concurrent hot sessions) — run in staging.

Action items (owners):
- Miguel: implement EW_grant_log + simple admission API (ETA 2w).
- Sofia: add KV eviction telemetry hook to host exporter and Console heatmap (ETA 1w).
- Jordan: create bench harness configs for Mix 1/2/3 and parameter sweep (ETA 1.5w).
- Anika: run initial canary and synth runs, collect results and iterate on Q and EW default (ETA 3w).

Quick notes to self (observational):
- Observed p99 spikes often correlate with KV eviction bursts after a large concurrent prefill rollout; prioritizing hot-session protection gave best subjective UX in manual tests.
- Small randomized delays often smooth peaks better than hard preemption.

References and related tickets:
- JIRA-RT-630 (kv eviction incident post-batch-rollout), JIRA-RT-710 (prefill scheduling primitives), PR#314 (microbatch boundaries instrumentation prototype).

Appendix: rough admission pseudocode (sketch):

// on decode token arrival
if host.soft_throttle == false:
  if host.kernel_util < soft_threshold:
    grant_EW(stream, default_EW)
  else:
    if random() < grant_prob_under_load:
      sleep(random(5..12)ms)
      grant_EW(stream, reduced_EW)
    else:
      enqueue_to_boundary(stream)
else: // soft throttle active
  sleep(random(6..16)ms)
  enqueue_to_boundary(stream)

// on microbatch boundary reached
serve_next_prefill_microbatch_or_resume_queued_streams()

End of doc.
